plain_title: Bedwetting past the age most children stay dry
one_liner: Repeated wetting of the bed or clothes, by day or night, in a child aged five or older.
in_simple_words: Enuresis is when a child aged five or older keeps wetting the bed or their clothes, at least twice a week for three months, and it isn't explained by a medical condition. Night-time bedwetting is by far the most common form. It's not laziness or naughtiness. Deep sleep, extra urine at night, constipation, and family history all play a part. Most children grow out of it, and simple treatments like bedwetting alarms work well.
what_it_can_feel_like: She was mortified about sleepovers. The alarm took about eight weeks and she hasn't looked back.
My dad wet the bed till he was ten, and so did I. Knowing that helped more than any chart.
We stopped the punishments once we understood he couldn't wake up. That changed the whole mood at home.
common_signs: Wetting the bed or clothes repeatedly, at age five or older
At least twice a week for three months, or causing real distress
Most often at night; sometimes in the day, or both
Not caused by a medical condition or medication
Often embarrassment, avoiding sleepovers, or low mood

myths_vs_facts.fact: Children who wet the bed are usually deeply asleep and can't feel the signal. It's a developmental and physical issue, not a behaviour choice.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Punishing or shaming will stop it.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Punishment makes bedwetting worse and harms the child. Guidelines are clear that children should never be punished for wetting.

myths_vs_facts.myth: You just have to wait it out.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Many children do grow out of it, but if it's upsetting the child, bedwetting alarms and sometimes medication help a lot and are worth asking about.

how_common.plain: About 1 in 5 children still wet the bed at five, 1 in 10 at six, and around 1 in 100 at fifteen or older. Almost all children grow out of it eventually.
how_common.figure: About 20% at age 5, 10% at age 6 (Raising Children Network); roughly 5%–10% of 5-year-olds (DSM-5-TR text); about 99% dry by 15 (Nationwide Children's)

what_helps.plain_summary: First steps are simple: treat constipation, keep daytime drinking regular, avoid caffeine, and never punish wetting. For children seven and over, or younger ones who are motivated, a bedwetting alarm is the first-line treatment in NICE guidance and has the best long-term results. Desmopressin, a medication that reduces night-time urine, can be prescribed and monitored by a doctor for quick results or special occasions. A doctor checks for urine infection, diabetes, or constipation first.
evidence_based_options: Treating constipation and reviewing fluids and toileting routine
Desmopressin prescribed and monitored by a doctor, when appropriate
Reward systems for agreed behaviours (like drinking well in the day), not for dry nights
self_help_that_supports_care: A calm, no-blame attitude: 'it's not your fault, and we'll fix it together'
Easy clean-up: waterproof mattress covers, spare sheets, the child helping without shame
Regular toilet visits before bed; no caffeine
Talking to the school and planning for trips and sleepovers

when_to_reach_out: If a child is five or older and still wetting, and it's upsetting them or you, ask a doctor, health visitor, school nurse, or continence service for help. See a doctor sooner if wetting starts again after months of being dry, or comes with pain, thirst, or daytime problems.
is_not: Wetting in children under five, occasional accidents, wetting caused by urine infection, diabetes, or constipation, and a sudden return of wetting after a stressful event are assessed separately.
hope_note: Almost every child becomes dry. With an alarm and patience, most do so within a few months.

in_young_people: Teens with enuresis often feel intense shame and hide it. It's still treatable at any age, and a doctor or continence service will have seen it many times.
